standard.title: Evaluate texts with comprehension strategies
standard.description: use comprehension strategies when listening and viewing to build literal and inferred meaning to evaluate information and ideas in texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students use comprehension strategies to build literal and inferred meaning across texts (AC9E2LY05). They have not yet used comprehension strategies specifically to evaluate information and ideas — assessing relevance, importance and accuracy.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use comprehension strategies when listening and viewing to build literal and inferred meaning and evaluate information and ideas in texts.

nodes.label: Building literal and inferred meaning
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use comprehension strategies including prediction, questioning and inference to build both literal and inferred meaning from texts.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply at least two comprehension strategies (e.g. predicting, inferring, questioning) to build meaning from a text, explaining what each strategy helped them understand.
nodes.typical_width: Make predictions about a text; determine important ideas, events or details; draw inferences using text evidence and prior knowledge; learn new content and ask questions to expand understanding.
wider: Compare comprehension strategies used for narrative versus informative texts, discussing how purpose changes which strategies are most useful
Revisit predictions made before reading after completing a text and discuss whether and why they were confirmed or revised
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not built literal and inferred meaning using comprehension strategies cannot evaluate information and ideas at N2 — evaluation is downstream of comprehension, not parallel to it.

response_modes.reason: Students at Y3 benefit from building a repertoire of named strategies that they can select and apply. Familiarity with multiple strategies — rather than defaulting to one — expands their comprehension toolkit across different text types.

success_criteria: Student applies at least two named comprehension strategies to a text
Student distinguishes between information stated directly (literal) and meaning they had to work out (inferred)

nodes.label: Evaluating information and ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate information and ideas in texts — assessing relevance for a task, comparing how different texts present similar ideas, and determining importance.
nodes.minimum_width: Make at least one evaluative judgement about a text — e.g. whether it is relevant for a task, which information is most important, or whether two texts agree — and explain the reasoning.
nodes.typical_width: Compare and contrast how different texts present similar ideas or information; determine the relevance of a text for a particular task; evaluate information and ideas across texts when listening and viewing.
wider: Compare two texts that present conflicting information about the same topic and discuss how to decide which to trust
Evaluate which source (a book, a video, a website) is most useful for a specific research purpose and justify the choice

response_modes.reason: Evaluation requires criteria — students need reasoning scaffolds for what makes information important, relevant or trustworthy at Y3. Without criteria, evaluation defaults to preference. The reasoning structure (relevant/important/accurate because...) needs explicit modelling.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Evaluating information across sources is directly relevant to inquiry and research tasks at Y3, and the elaboration explicitly includes multi-text comparison. Advancing students can engage with the concept that not all sources say the same thing — a foundational critical literacy insight.
success_criteria: Student makes an evaluative judgement about a text (relevant/important/trustworthy) and gives a reason
Student's reason is connected to a specific feature of the text — not just a general impression
